readerTitle: Why the plumber who explains wins the job
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Bickman 1974 제복 실험, Martin·Goldstein·Cialdini 부동산 사무실 사례) + 가상 사례 (배관 업체, 사이버보안 컨설팅)
insight: 권위는 '최고'라고 주장하는 것이 아니라, 고객이 품질을 판단할 수 없는 순간에 그 문제와 관련된 전문성을 구체적으로 먼저 보여주는 것이다.
misconception: 자격증, 수상 경력, 유명인 이름을 많이 내걸수록 신뢰가 쌓인다. 혹은 권위는 큰 회사만 가질 수 있다.

sources.text: Cialdini, R. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. (Authority as a principle of influence)
Bickman, L. (1974). The Social Power of a Uniform. Journal of Applied Social Psychology.
Martin, S., Goldstein, N., & Cialdini, R. (2014). The Small BIG. (Real estate office introducing agents' experience)

factChecks.note: 부동산 사무실 사례: 접수 직원이 상담 연결 전에 중개인의 경력을 소개하자 상담 예약과 계약이 늘었다는 내용은 The Small BIG(2014)에 나옵니다. 구체적 증가율(예약 약 20%, 계약 약 15%로 알려짐)은 원문 확인 전이라 카드에 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원문으로 확인하세요.
Bickman(1974): 경비원 제복을 입은 실험자의 요청에 행인이 더 많이 따랐다는 결과입니다. 수치는 생략하고 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 실험 세부 조건을 원문으로 확인하세요.
배관 업체와 사이버보안 컨설팅 사례는 모두 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치는 없습니다.

cards.title: Why the plumber who explains wins the job
body: Your water heater dies. Two plumbers come out. Both quote about the same price.
The first says, "I can replace it Thursday." The second taps the tank and says, "See this rust line? That's sediment. I see it a lot in this neighborhood. Here's how we stop it happening again."
You already know who you're calling back.

image.label: Two plumbers beside a broken water heater, one pointing and explaining
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 지하실의 고장 난 온수기 앞에 배관공 두 명. 한 명은 클립보드만 들고 서 있고, 다른 한 명은 온수기의 녹 자국을 가리키며 집주인에게 설명 중. 집주인의 시선은 설명하는 배관공 쪽. 실제 회사 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Customers keep picking someone else.
body: You run a home repair company. Most customers collect three quotes, and you lose many jobs where your price was fair.
You have budget for one change this month. Which one?

options.text: Cut prices by 10% to stand out
options.feedback: You may win more jobs, but you give up margin on every one. And customers who can't judge quality often read a lower price as lower skill.

options.text: Train techs to explain the cause and mention similar jobs they've done, before quoting
options.feedback: This shows relevant expertise right when the customer is unsure. It costs a little time per visit, not margin.

options.text: Put a big "Award-winning service" badge on the vans
options.feedback: Visible, and better than nothing. But a vague badge says little about this customer's problem, so it carries less weight.

cards.title: A short introduction changed who got the meeting.
body: Researchers Steve Martin, Noah Goldstein and Robert Cialdini describe a real estate office that made one small change. When callers asked about selling, the receptionist no longer just said, "I'll put you through."
Instead she named the agent and their experience in that kind of property before connecting the call. The authors report that appointments and signed contracts both went up.
Nobody gained new skills. The office simply made existing expertise visible at the moment the customer was deciding.

cards.title: Authority
body: **Authority** is our tendency to follow people who seem to know more than we do, especially when we can't judge the quality ourselves.

Most customers can't inspect a water heater, an audit or a legal contract. So they look for signs of expertise instead. Psychologist Robert Cialdini named authority as one of the main principles of influence in his 1984 book *Influence*.

image.label: Customer uncertain about quality, looking to an expert's evidence
image.brief: 개념 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 물음표가 떠 있는 고객, 가운데 "Can't judge quality" 라벨, 오른쪽에 전문가가 들고 있는 세 개의 카드 "Relevant", "Shown early", "Specific". 화살표가 고객에서 전문가 쪽으로. 단순하고 밝은 색.

cards.title: Three things make authority land.
body: Credentials hidden on an "About us" page rarely do much. Authority persuades when it is:
list: **Relevant:** expertise in *this* problem, not general prestige
**Early:** shown before the price, while the customer is still unsure
**Specific:** a diagnosis, a number of similar jobs, a named person, not "experts you can trust"
cards.callout: The plumber's rust line beats a wall of certificates.

cards.title: Saying "you don't need that" builds authority.
body: An expert who argues against their own interest looks more credible. A mechanic who says, "Your brakes have another year, don't pay me for them yet," earns belief for the next recommendation.
Admitting a limit works the same way. "This isn't our specialty, but here's who is" signals you care more about the right answer than the sale.
cards.softwareNote: In software, authority shows up as a support reply that pinpoints the cause, a setup guide written by someone who clearly knows the user's industry, or a sales call that recommends the cheaper plan when it fits.

cards.title: Borrowed authority can backfire.
body: Signs of authority work even when they shouldn't. In a 1974 study by Leonard Bickman, people on the street obeyed odd requests more often when the person asking wore a guard's uniform.

That power is easy to misuse: actors in lab coats, a celebrity praising something they know nothing about, inflated titles. Customers who spot it don't just ignore the claim. They stop trusting everything else you say.
Only claim expertise you can back up on the spot.

cards.title: Now it's a cybersecurity consultancy.
body: Your five-person firm is pitching a mid-sized manufacturer. Their operations director worries about ransomware but can't tell good security advice from bad.
How do you open the meeting?

options.text: Show a slide of 40 client logos and industry awards
options.feedback: It signals that others trust you, which helps. But it doesn't show you understand a factory floor, so the director still can't judge your skill.

options.text: Share two specific risks you found in a quick review of their setup, and introduce the consultant who has secured other plants
options.feedback: Relevant, early and specific. It takes prep time before the meeting, but it lets the buyer see expertise instead of taking it on faith.

options.text: Lead with a famous former executive you just added as an advisor
options.feedback: A big name grabs attention. If that person won't do the work and knows little about factories, it reads as borrowed authority.

cards.title: Show your expertise where the doubt is.
body: Customers who can't judge quality look for an expert. Be that expert visibly: relevant, early and specific, and honest about your limits.
**Try it today:** write down the moment your customers feel most unsure. Add one sentence there that shows real, specific experience with their exact problem.
